sections.html:
Manchester sits on the Merrimack River in south-central New Hampshire, about 20 miles from the Massachusetts border and 58 miles from Boston. The city is in Hillsborough County, which shares its county seat role between Manchester and Nashua, and it had 115,644 residents in 2020. Commuters to Boston and Concord are a real part of the buyer pool. Roughly half of occupied homes are rented, so a sale often involves tenants or a landlord who owns more than one property.

The city's 2010 Master Plan divides it into 25 neighborhoods, and assessments and house styles change a lot from one to the next.

  • West Side: Amoskeag, Rimmon Heights, Notre Dame/McGregorville, and Piscataquog/Granite Square
  • East Side: North End, Janeville/Corey Square, Hallsville, and Bakersville
  • Outer areas: Youngsville and Goffes Falls

A West Side seller and a Goffes Falls seller deal with the same Board of Assessors and Tax Collector, but the buyer pool and the age of the housing can look very different.

The mills defined Manchester for a century after it incorporated as a city in 1846, so the housing stock is older than most. An older house is more likely to need work before it shows well.

  • Older roofs and chimneys take freeze and thaw cycles every year.
  • Heating systems in 1960s houses are often original or near the end of their life.
  • Homes near the Merrimack, the Piscataquog or Cohas Brook deserve a look at the basement and the flood zone status before listing.

A cash buyer prices these items in directly, which is why many owners with deferred repairs choose an as-is sale.

The property tax year runs April 1 to March 31 under RSA 76:2, and taxes are assessed on the inventory taken that April. The Board of Assessors sets the value, and the Office of the Tax Collector bills it.

The Assessors estimate value three ways: recent sales of comparable properties, replacement cost less depreciation, and, for income property such as apartments, an income approach. The tax rate is the levy divided by total assessed value, and the same rate applies to every owner. The state Department of Revenue Administration issues the rate in October or November.

Bills go out twice a year. The first, mailed in early June, is based on half of the previous year's rate. The second, mailed in late November, uses the new rate and any assessment changes. Each bill is due 30 days after it is issued. The 2025 rate is 20.24 per $1,000, up from 19.58 for 2024, and a separate Central Business Service District rate of 0.462730 applies for 2025.

Unpaid tax moves from interest to a lien in about a year and can end in a city tax deed after two years.

StepWhat happens
Interest8 percent per year on late taxes (RSA 76:13)
Notice of ArrearageSent about 30 days after each billing (RSA 76:11-b)
Notice of Impending LienCertified mail at least 30 days before the lien is executed (RSA 80:60)
Lien executedInterest becomes 14 percent per year (RSA 80:69); lien recorded at the Registry of Deeds within 30 days
Mortgagee noticeSent 60 days after execution, with a $10 fee plus any title search cost (RSA 80:67)
Tax deedIf unpaid two years after execution, with a notice of impending deed at least 30 days earlier (RSA 80:76, 80:77)

After a deed, a prior owner or mortgagee who wants to reclaim the property must notify the city by certified mail within 30 days of the notice of intent to repurchase. They have to show they can pay the back taxes, interest, costs and a penalty of 10 percent of the equalized assessed value (RSA 80:89).

Send a written abatement application to the Board of Assessors so that it is received or postmarked by March 1 after the final tax bill. It cannot be filed online because an original signature is required, and there is no filing fee with the city.

You must be the owner of record on April 1 of the tax year, or otherwise an aggrieved party, and you carry the burden of showing the property was assessed disproportionately compared with other property in town. The Board has until July 1 to decide. If it says nothing by then, the application is treated as denied.

  • Further appeal is due by September 1.
  • Choose one route: the State Board of Tax and Land Appeals (written, with a fee) or Hillsborough County Superior Court, Northern District, 300 Chestnut Street, Manchester.
  • Filing with the Board of Tax and Land Appeals waives the right to petition the Superior Court (RSA 76-B:11).

If you are selling and think the value is wrong, mention the pending application to the title company, since the outcome affects the tax bill for the year you owned the house.

Tell the title company at the start, because unpaid tax and any recorded lien are paid out of the sale proceeds at closing. The Tax Collector can provide a copy of a lien release for $10 per property plus $2 per receipt requested, by email at Taxcollector@manchesternh.gov or in person at One City Hall Plaza.

Redeemed liens are released within 30 days, and the release is mailed to the Hillsborough County Register of Deeds, 19 Temple Street, Nashua. A new deed can take 30 days or more to reach the Assessors, so the bill may still carry your name after closing. Pass new-owner and address information along in writing.

New Hampshire's real estate transfer tax is $0.75 per $100 of the price, paid by both the buyer and the seller, with a $20 minimum each when the price is $4,000 or less. Stamps are bought from the register of deeds. The Purchaser's and Seller's Declarations of Consideration (CD-57-P and CD-57-S) and the PA-34 inventory are due to the state within 30 days after the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: When is Manchester property tax due?
faqs.a: Two bills a year, each due 30 days after it is issued. The first goes out in early June and the second in late November. The tax year runs April 1 to March 31.

faqs.q: What is the interest rate on late Manchester property tax?
faqs.a: 8 percent per year on unpaid taxes under RSA 76:13. Once a tax lien is executed, interest on the lien is 14 percent per year under RSA 80:69.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Manchester house if there is a tax lien on it?
faqs.a: Yes. The lien is paid from the sale proceeds and released after payment, and a full redemption leads to a release within 30 days. Ask the Tax Collector for the current payoff before closing.

faqs.q: Who pays the New Hampshire transfer tax when a house sells?
faqs.a: Both sides do. The rate is $0.75 per $100 of the price for each of the buyer and the seller, and transfers by will or intestate succession are exempt.

faqs.q: Where do I appeal a Manchester assessment after the Board of Assessors denies it?
faqs.a: File by September 1 with either the State Board of Tax and Land Appeals or Hillsborough County Superior Court, Northern District. You pick one, and choosing the state board waives the court option.
